child_drafts.title: Trump declares a national emergency at the southern border
child_drafts.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump declared a national emergency at the southern border and made military support authorities available for the federal response.
child_drafts.description_medium: The proclamation invoked the National Emergencies Act and specified Title 10 authorities. It made use of the Armed Forces available to support the government response and invoked construction authority for the Defense Secretary. The document also revoked the 2021 proclamation that had terminated the prior southern-border emergency.
child_drafts.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation declaring a national emergency at the southern border. The proclamation invoked the National Emergencies Act and made specified Title 10 authorities available to the military departments under the Defense Secretary’s direction. It stated that Armed Forces support was required and invoked 10 U.S.C. § 2808 construction authority for the Defense Secretary. It also revoked the January 2021 proclamation that had terminated the earlier border emergency and redirected border-wall funds. The proclamation describes a federal border response, including military support; its text identifies that emergency as the southern-border emergency.

child_drafts.title: Trump declares a separate national energy emergency
child_drafts.description_short: On January 20, 2025, Trump separately declared a national energy emergency and directed agencies to use lawful authorities to facilitate domestic energy production and infrastructure.
child_drafts.description_medium: The order directed federal agencies to identify and exercise available emergency and other lawful authorities for energy leasing, siting, production, transportation, refining, and generation. It also called for expedited agency review of qualifying submissions, including specified Endangered Species Act procedures. It focused on domestic resources, including those on federal lands.
child_drafts.description_long: A separate executive order dated January 20, 2025, declared a national energy emergency. It directed agency heads to identify and exercise lawful emergency and other authorities to facilitate identification, leasing, siting, production, transportation, refining, and generation of domestic energy resources, including on federal lands. The order directed the Interior Secretary, to the extent practicable under law, to review certain submissions promptly, identify legal deficiencies, and provide an initial determination within 20 days. It described a process for convening the Endangered Species Act Committee to resolve qualifying submissions within 140 days of eligibility determination. The order’s stated aim was facilitating domestic energy supply and infrastructure under existing legal authority.

child_drafts.title: Israel launches strikes against Iran
child_drafts.description_short: Israel launched strikes against Iran on June 13, 2025; Iran retaliated with missile attacks, Reuters reported.
child_drafts.description_medium: Reuters’ contemporaneous coverage described an Israeli campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets amid tensions over Iran’s nuclear program. Iran responded with missile attacks, with explosions reported in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. This was the opening Israeli action, separate from the later U.S. strikes.
child_drafts.description_long: Israel began strikes against Iran on June 13, 2025, targeting nuclear and military infrastructure amid tensions over Iran’s nuclear program. Reuters reported that Iran retaliated that night with missile salvos, with explosions heard in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv. Israel’s military said fewer than 100 missiles had been fired and that most were intercepted or fell short; U.S. forces helped shoot down some missiles headed toward Israel, according to U.S. officials. The International Atomic Energy Agency chief told the U.N. Security Council that the above-ground pilot enrichment plant at Natanz had been destroyed, while the extent of damage at other sites was still being assessed. Reuters also reported the deaths of senior Iranian commanders and nuclear scientists, attributing casualty figures to Iranian officials.

The extent of damage remained uncertain in contemporaneous reporting, so claims that the sites were wholly destroyed require qualification.
child_drafts.description_long: U.S. forces struck the Iranian nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan during the night of June 21 into June 22, 2025. Reuters reported that B-2 bombers and other U.S. weapons were used, including bunker-buster bombs at Fordow and Tomahawk missiles. Iranian officials confirmed an attack on Fordow. President Trump described the sites as obliterated, but contemporaneous damage assessments remained uncertain, and the Reuters report recorded questions about the scale of damage. The operation followed Israel’s June 13 campaign and was conducted by U.S. forces as a separate action. The two dates, military actors, aircraft, weapons, and targets formed separate stages in the broader conflict.

child_drafts.title: Administration cancels about $400 million in Columbia grants and contracts
child_drafts.description_short: On March 7, 2025, federal agencies announced cancellation of about $400 million in Columbia University grants and contracts, citing antisemitic harassment allegations.
child_drafts.description_medium: The administration described the cancellations as a response to antisemitic harassment on and near Columbia’s New York campus. Reuters reported that much of the funding supported health care and scientific research, but it could not independently verify the stated amount. Civil-rights groups questioned the action’s process and constitutionality.
child_drafts.description_long: On March 7, 2025, the Trump administration announced immediate cancellation of about $400 million in federal grants and contracts to Columbia University. The administration said the action responded to antisemitic harassment on and near the university’s New York City campus. Reuters reported that much of the affected funding supported health care and scientific research, but said it could not independently verify the amount. Civil-rights groups criticized the cancellations as lacking due process and as punishment of protected speech; those were attributed criticisms rather than a court ruling. The announcement concerned Columbia and its federal funding commitments, which Reuters said exceeded $5 billion. Federal officials did not identify the particular grants and contracts targeted in the initial announcement.

child_drafts.title: Federal officials send Columbia a letter setting conditions tied to campus policy
child_drafts.description_short: Federal officials sent Columbia University a letter dated March 13, 2025, outlining conditions connected to the administration’s funding dispute.
child_drafts.description_medium: Reuters reported that federal officials sent Columbia’s interim president and trustees a March 13 letter listing nine demands concerning protest rules and university governance. They included a ban on face masks, arrest powers for campus security, and five-year academic receivership for a department. The demands were preconditions for funding talks.
child_drafts.description_long: A two-page letter from federal officials to Columbia University’s interim president and trustees, sent March 13, 2025, set out conditions tied to the administration’s campus-protest dispute and suspended federal funding. Reuters reported that the administration demanded a campus face-mask ban, arrest powers for university security, changes to admissions policies, and adoption of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism. It also sought academic receivership for at least five years over Columbia’s Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African Studies department. The letter did not explain why that department was singled out. The administration described the nine demands as preconditions for opening talks about restoring $400 million in federal funding. Columbia’s shared-governance process would require some policy changes to pass its University Senate, Reuters reported.

corrected_draft.description_long: DOJ’s official clemency records list former Border Patrol agents Jose Alonso Compean and Ignacio Ramos among President Trump’s December 22, 2020, pardons. These pardons occurred during Trump’s first term. DOJ separately lists a January 20, 2025 proclamation granting clemency for certain offenses related to the January 6, 2021, Capitol events; it is a different clemency action.

corrected_draft.description_short: On January 29, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed creation of a task force to review military personnel policies, including hiring, promotion, and selection.

Hegseth set a March 1 interim report deadline and a June 1 final report deadline for the task force.
corrected_draft.description_long: On January 29, 2025, the Defense Department announced that Secretary Pete Hegseth had directed a task force on restoring the department’s fighting force. The department said hiring, promotion, and assignment decisions should be based on merit, the department’s needs, and individual preferences. The task force was assigned to examine personnel policies and recommend changes. Hegseth set March 1 as a deadline for an interim report and June 1 for a final report on the task force’s activities. The announcement framed the work as reviewing military personnel policy and force readiness. It did not describe a political loyalty criterion. The department’s stated standard for personnel decisions in the announcement was merit-based, alongside institutional needs and the individual’s preferences.
